topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Whole numbers
topic.scope: natural vs whole numbers, number line, properties of operations, identity elements, patterns

misconceptions.statement: Zero is a natural number because it is a number.
misconceptions.why: Students conflate the set of all numbers with the specific set of counting numbers.
misconceptions.fix: Natural numbers are counting numbers starting from 1. Whole numbers include 0 and all natural numbers.

probe.question: Which of these is the smallest natural number: 0 or 1?

misconceptions.root_belief: All numbers belong to the same category
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

misconceptions.statement: a - b is the same as b - a.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the commutative property of addition to all operations.
misconceptions.fix: Subtraction is not commutative; changing the order of numbers changes the result.
misconceptions.root_belief: A rule from one operation works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The identity element for subtraction is 0.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the additive identity (0) with the identity property itself.
misconceptions.fix: There is no identity element for subtraction because subtracting 0 from a number keeps it the same, but subtracting a number from 0 does not.

probe.question: What number can be subtracted from 7 to keep it 7?

misconceptions.root_belief: One property applies to all operations

misconceptions.statement: Natural numbers are the numbers that come after zero and stop at some big number like 100 or 1000.
misconceptions.why: Students meet only small counting numbers in practice and think 'counting numbers' must end somewhere.
misconceptions.fix: Natural numbers 1, 2, 3, ... go on forever; there is no largest natural number, because adding 1 always gives a bigger one.

probe.question: What is the greatest natural number?
probe.wrong_answer: 1000 (or some very big number like a crore)

misconceptions.root_belief: Counting numbers must end at some largest number

misconceptions.statement: The smallest natural number is 0 because nothing is less than zero when counting.
misconceptions.why: Students use 0 as the starting point of counting and mix 'starting count' with 'counting numbers'.
misconceptions.fix: Natural numbers are the counting numbers starting from 1, so the smallest natural number is 1; 0 is the smallest whole number.

probe.question: Write the smallest natural number and the smallest whole number.

misconceptions.root_belief: Smallest number in any list must be zero

misconceptions.statement: Whole numbers include negative numbers like -1 and -2 as well.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'whole' means all numbers of the number line, and negatives look like whole numbers with a sign.
misconceptions.fix: Whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, ... only; negative numbers are not whole numbers (they come later as integers).

probe.question: Is -5 a whole number? Say yes or no.
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a complete number without a fraction

misconceptions.root_belief: Whole means any complete number, including negatives

misconceptions.statement: Whole numbers are just natural numbers, so there is no difference between the two sets.
misconceptions.why: Both sets look alike in everyday use and 0 seems unimportant, so students treat the names as synonyms.
misconceptions.fix: Whole numbers = natural numbers together with 0; every natural number is whole but 0 is whole and not natural.

probe.question: Which whole number is not a natural number?
probe.wrong_answer: None, all whole numbers are natural numbers

misconceptions.root_belief: Different names for number sets mean the same set

misconceptions.statement: Numbers with more digits-in-zeros or a bigger-looking first digit are always to the right, so 9 is to the right of 10.
misconceptions.why: Students compare by the first digit seen and ignore the number of digits and place value.
misconceptions.fix: On the number line a number with more digits is greater than one with fewer digits (for whole numbers), so 10 lies to the right of 9.

probe.question: Which is greater and lies to the right on the number line: 9 or 10?

misconceptions.root_belief: Compare numbers by their first digit only

misconceptions.statement: The number line starts at 0 and the arrow shows it ends, so numbers cannot continue to the right.
misconceptions.why: Textbook drawings show a finite segment with ticks up to 10 or 20, taken as the whole line.
misconceptions.fix: The arrow on the right means the number line continues forever; we can always mark bigger whole numbers further right.

probe.question: Can we mark 100 on a number line that was drawn from 0 to 10?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the line ends at 10 so 100 cannot be shown

misconceptions.root_belief: A drawn number line is finite as shown

misconceptions.statement: Whole numbers are closed under subtraction, since subtracting two whole numbers always gives a whole number.
misconceptions.why: Students try only examples like 8 - 3 and overgeneralise without testing a smaller number minus a bigger one.
misconceptions.fix: Whole numbers are closed under addition and multiplication but not subtraction; for example 3 - 8 is not a whole number.

probe.question: Is 4 - 9 a whole number? Is the set closed under subtraction?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 4 - 9 = 5 so it is a whole number and the set is closed

misconceptions.root_belief: A rule that works in some examples works always
misconceptions.source_hint: research on negative number and subtraction errors

misconceptions.statement: The identity element for multiplication is 0, because multiplying by 0 leaves the number unchanged.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over 'add 0 changes nothing' to multiplication without checking what 0 does.
misconceptions.fix: The multiplicative identity is 1, since a x 1 = a; multiplying by 0 always gives 0.
misconceptions.root_belief: Identity is always zero for every operation

misconceptions.statement: Division of whole numbers is commutative, so 12 ÷ 4 is the same as 4 ÷ 12.
misconceptions.why: Students see that addition and multiplication can be swapped and assume every operation can be swapped.
misconceptions.fix: Only addition and multiplication are commutative; 12 ÷ 4 = 3 but 4 ÷ 12 is not even a whole number.
